strengths: Novel and elegant integration of RoPE with finite Platonic symmetry groups, yielding a principled weight-sharing scheme and group-equivariant linear layers while keeping the attention computation graph and cost close to a standard Transformer.

Theoretical analysis provides useful insights: formal equivalence of linear RoPE attention with constant keys to a dynamic convolution and its extension to dynamic group convolution; the proofs in the appendices are generally sound.
Strong reproducibility effort: code is provided, with detailed hyperparameters, training details, and compute budgets in the appendices.

Demonstrates practical speed benefits: inference times are comparable to a standard Transformer and much faster than G-Hyena/TFN; the Fourier-domain implementation shows potential for further efficiency gains.
The idea has clear potential for AI4Science and geometric deep learning by making approximate equivariance scalable and relatively cheap.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is limited and does not fully support the claim of competitive performance. CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN gains are marginal (e.g., CIFAR-10 attention 91.49% to 92.73%; ScanObjectNN 80.5% to 81.3/82.0%) and far from state-of-the-art; no comparison to strong equivariant or standard baselines on these tasks.
QM9 experiments report only two of the standard 12 targets (mu and alpha), which is selective and insufficient to claim broad competitiveness; comparison to many strong E(3) baselines is missing.

The OMol25 comparison is problematic: the reproduced eSEN under 120 hours is much worse than literature (force 23.92 vs 10.11; energy 120.0 vs 29.8), indicating under-training. Claiming superiority under identical conditions is not meaningful when the baseline is not converged, and comparison to literature numbers with different budgets is not apples-to-apples.

The theoretical equivalence to dynamic convolution assumes softmax is omitted and keys are constant (k_j=1). It is unclear how much this applies to the actual attention model; fixing keys is a significant architectural restriction and departs from standard attention. The abstract overclaims 'this attention is formally equivalent to a dynamic group convolution' without these caveats.

Equivariance is only to a finite discrete subgroup of SO(3)/O(3), not full continuous SO(3)/E(3). Calling it 'approximate E(n)' is fair, but the paper sometimes overclaims full Euclidean equivariance, and there is no error analysis for rotations outside the group.

Implementation details of the group convolutions are insufficiently specified (e.g., how structured weight matrices are materialized, initialization, memory overhead), and it is unclear how key fixing is handled in attention versus convolution modes.
There is no dedicated limitations section; failure cases, approximation error, and computational/memory overhead due to the group axis are not discussed.

Presentation has issues: related work in the main text is thin (Appendix B is largely a list of names), and there are inconsistencies/typos (e.g., 'Flop' for flip, 'Platonic' vs 'platonic', Table 5 formatting) that reduce clarity.

strengths: Introduces a principled method to combine RoPE with finite subgroup reference frames, yielding a weight-sharing scheme and group-convolution equivariant linear layers that preserve a standard Transformer-like computation graph.

Provides formal theoretical results: a group-theoretic derivation of RoPE, an end-to-end equivariance proof for the proposed architecture, an equivalence between linear RoPE attention and dynamic convolution, and linear-time complexity for the convolutional variant.
The method can reduce parameter count through weight-sharing while maintaining FLOPs comparable to a standard Transformer with the same effective feature dimension.
The paper includes a reproducibility statement, source code, and extensive appendices with hyperparameters and training details.
Some limitations are honestly discussed, such as the instability of learned keys on molecular tasks and the approximate nature of the discrete-group equivariance.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is too weak to support the central claim of competitive performance. On CIFAR-10 the model reaches only ~92.7% and on ScanObjectNN ~82%, which are far below standard state-of-the-art results; no external baselines (e.g., standard ViT, Point-MAE, Point Transformer) are compared on these tasks.

The OMol25 comparison is not convincing: the authors' own eSEN baseline under the same 120-hour budget is far worse than the literature eSEN (Energy 120 vs 29.8, Force 23.9 vs 10.1), and the Platonic Transformer (Force 24.25, Energy 74.0) is substantially worse than MACE and eSEN from the literature. The claim of 'highly competitive' force prediction is unsupported.

QM9 results report only two of the twelve standard targets (μ and α), making it impossible to assess overall performance against established benchmarks; the claim of being 'on par with SOTA' is not substantiated across the full task.
Main tables lack error bars, variance, or statistical significance, making it difficult to judge whether small gains over the trivial-group baseline are meaningful.

Several claims are overstated. The abstract says the method preserves the 'exact architecture' of a standard Transformer, but it introduces a group axis, group-convolution linear layers, per-frame attention heads, and sometimes constant keys or APE, so the model is not an exact standard Transformer.

Equivariance is only to a finite discrete subgroup, but the paper often frames this as approximate E(3)/SE(3) equivariance without measuring rotation-equivariance error or testing on continuous rotations outside the chosen group. In 3D, only rotational subgroups are used, not full reflection groups, further weakening E(3) claims.

The linear-time convolutional variant suffers large accuracy drops (e.g., CIFAR-10 88.6 vs 91.5), and its scalability benefit is not demonstrated on genuinely long-sequence or large-scale tasks; the paper does not show that this trade-off is worthwhile in practice.

The handling of keys is unclear and inconsistent: the dynamic-convolution result assumes constant keys, and the authors mention using fixed keys for QM9/OMol25, which deviates from standard attention and may affect fairness and comparability.

The paper contains presentation issues and reference errors (e.g., 'attu' instead of 'attn', mismatched author names/years, typos in the appendix), and some experimental details such as frame selection for vision tasks are not fully specified.

The limitations discussion is incomplete: it does not address the gap to state-of-the-art results, the computational cost of group convolution for large groups, or the loss of continuous rotational equivariance in practice.

strengths: Introduces the Platonic Transformer, a novel and elegant way to inject discrete roto-reflection equivariance into standard Transformers by defining RoPE attention relative to reference frames from Platonic solid symmetry groups, while preserving the standard computation graph and computational cost.

Provides a solid theoretical foundation: formalizes RoPE from group representation theory, proves end-to-end equivariance of the attention mechanism, and shows equivalence to a dynamic group convolution with linear-time complexity.

Demonstrates broad empirical applicability across computer vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction (QM9, OMol25), with QM9 results matching state-of-the-art EquiformerV2 on μ and α targets.

Shows practical efficiency: inference time is within the same order of magnitude as a standard Transformer and orders of magnitude faster than G-Hyena and Tensor Field Networks, while retaining E(3)-like equivariance.
Good reproducibility: source code is provided, and appendices give detailed hyperparameters, training protocols, and proofs.
The Fourier-domain implementation discussion (Appendix M) provides useful insight into potential future scaling and connections to steerable networks.
weaknesses: The central claim of resolving the symmetry-awareness vs. scaling trade-off is not fully substantiated. The method achieves approximate equivariance only to discrete subgroups (e.g., tetrahedral, octahedral) rather than full continuous E(3) or SO(3) equivariance, and the large-scale OMol25 results are far from literature SOTA (e.g., force MAE 24.25 vs. 10.11 for eSEN), relying on an under-budget comparison.

Experimental comparisons are confounded in key places. On CIFAR-10, the equivariant C4 model improves accuracy from 91.49% to 92.73% over the trivial-group baseline, but the models have very different parameter counts (85.1M vs. 21.3M), so gains may stem from regularization or parameter reduction rather than equivariance alone. No parameter-matched non-equivariant baseline is provided.

The QM9 evaluation is limited to only two target properties (μ and α), whereas QM9 benchmarks commonly report many more. Some baselines (e.g., FAFormer, G-Hyena) may not be well-suited to QM9 or may be undertuned, making the comparisons less informative.

The dynamic convolution equivalence (Proposition 2) relies on a special case: constant key vectors (k_j=1) and omission of softmax. The claim that fixing keys acts as a 'crucial regularizer' is supported mainly by anecdotal instability of mixed kernels, without rigorous analysis or ablation.

The linear-time convolutional variant is not used in the large-scale OMol25 experiment, undermining the scalability claim. It is also consistently worse than the attention variant on CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN, with only comparable performance on QM9.

Limitations are discussed only briefly. There is no thorough discussion of when discrete symmetry groups are insufficient, potential negative impacts when no symmetry is present, or the practical overhead of group convolutions. The 'no additional cost' claim assumes matching total head count and effective feature dimension, which may not hold in all deployment settings.

Presentation has minor issues: typos such as 'Flop' instead of 'Flip' and 'attu' instead of 'attn', and some implementation details (e.g., whether OMol25 uses attention or convolution) are not clearly stated in the main text.

strengths: The paper introduces a principled and elegant method to endow Transformers with discrete roto-translation equivariance by lifting features to reference frames of Platonic symmetry groups and applying RoPE per frame, preserving the standard attention computation graph.

The theoretical analysis is strong: it proves end-to-end equivariance (Prop. 3.1, App. B), establishes a connection to dynamic group convolution (Prop. 4.1), and derives a linear-time convolutional variant (Cor. 4.3).

Empirical evaluation is broad, covering vision (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, ImageNet), 3D point clouds, molecular generation (QM9), property prediction, large-scale OMol25, and ProteinMD. Results show consistent gains over translation-only baselines and competitive performance on several molecular benchmarks.
The method maintains computational cost comparable to a standard Transformer while reducing parameter count via weight sharing, and the linear-time variant offers scalability.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameter tables and open-source code (though the link is not visible in the manuscript).
Limitations are honestly discussed, including the restriction to discrete subgroups and uncharacterized extreme-scale behavior.
weaknesses: Overclaiming: The abstract and introduction state that the attention is 'formally equivalent to a dynamic group convolution' without noting the constant-key requirement; the equivalence does not hold for learned keys used in OMol25.

The claim of 'competitive performance relative to task-specific SOTA' is not supported for CIFAR-10, where 92.78% is far below SOTA, and no external SOTA baselines are provided for CIFAR-10 or ScanObjectNN.

The OMol25 comparison is not capacity-controlled: a 60M-parameter Platonic Transformer is compared against a 6M-parameter eSEN-sm baseline, making the 'outperforming SOTA' claim less convincing. Larger eSEN variants are not evaluated.

The linear convolutional variant is consistently 5–6 percentage points worse than the attention variant on CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN, yet its practical utility and the source of this gap are not adequately analyzed.

Presentation issues: notation inconsistency in Eq. 7 (\hat R vs \tilde R), citation numbering errors (e.g., eSEN-sm cited as [39] but [39] is ZATOM-1; G-Hyena cited as [46] but [46] is Qu & Krishnapriyan), and the abstract/intro mention roto-reflection equivariance while 3D experiments use only rotational subgroups.
The paper only guarantees equivariance to discrete subgroups of O(n); the approximation quality to full E(n) is not thoroughly quantified, although an equivariance error table is provided.

strengths: The core idea is clean and principled: representing features relative to a finite set of reference frames (Platonic symmetry groups) and applying unmodified RoPE per-frame yields a weight-sharing scheme that keeps the Transformer's computation graph essentially intact. This is an elegant way to inject geometric inductive bias without exotic modules.

Formal end-to-end equivariance to a discrete subgroup G ⊂ O(n) is stated and proven (Prop. 3.1, App. B), and the group-convolution interpretation of the constrained linear layers (Sec. 3.3) is correct and well-explained.

The analysis connecting linear RoPE attention to a dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 4.1, App. C) is an interesting reframing, and the linear-time corollary (Cor. 4.3) is a legitimate practical benefit.

Experiments are broad, spanning image classification, point clouds, molecular property prediction, and molecular generation. The ProteinMD result (Table 6) beats G-Hyena and the G-Transformer baseline, and the OMol25 throughput (2.6×) is a genuine efficiency advantage.

Reproducibility is good: open-source code, detailed hyperparameters (Table 12), and careful training/optimization descriptions in the appendices. The limitations section is honest about scale and the finite-subgroup restriction.
weaknesses: The headline OMol25 comparison (Table 5) is not apples-to-apples: the Platonic Transformer has 60M parameters while the eSEN-sm baseline has 6M. The claimed superiority (force MAE 9.33 vs 12.64) may largely be a model-capacity effect, so the central scaling/efficiency claim is not well supported. A parameter- or FLOP-matched eSEN baseline is needed.

The recurring claim of 'no additional cost' and 'preserving the exact architecture and computational cost of a standard Transformer' is overstated. FLOPs for a single matrix-vector may match, but the model is fundamentally altered (weight-shared group convolutions, reduced parameter count by |G|), so the equivariant and standard models are not the same object and do not have equal capacity. The framing oversells the equivalence.

The dynamic-convolution equivalence (Prop. 4.1) holds only in the degenerate constant-key setting (k_j = 1). With learned keys the attention is not a pure convolution, so the interpretability claim is much narrower than presented. The authors acknowledge this only as a 'design choice'.

The linear-time complexity result (Cor. 4.3) is essentially standard linear attention (Performer-style), which is already well known; it is presented as a contribution but offers little novelty. Empirically, the convolutional/linear variant is 5–6 percentage points worse than attention (Tables 1, 2), so the 'highly scalable' variant is of limited practical value.

Equivariance is exact only for the chosen finite subgroup, not for E(n). Describing the model as 'approximately E(n)-equivariant' and the title/abstract as achieving a broad equivariance glosses over this approximation, and no quantitative analysis of how well the finite group approximates the continuous group is given (App. N.1 reports equivariance error only briefly).

On non-equivariant tasks (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN), the reported gains over the {e} baseline are small (e.g., 91.65→92.78 on CIFAR-10) and the argument that they stem from 'weight sharing rather than capacity' is not rigorously disentangled. The baselines are far larger (85.1M vs 14.2M params), leaving open the possibility that the smaller, more regularized models simply train better.

On QM9 regression (Table 10), the method is only competitive on two targets (Δε and μ) and is clearly worse than specialized architectures on most others, which the authors acknowledge but which undercuts the abstract's claim of 'competitive performance' across benchmarks.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work by the same group and others (Bökman et al. 2025 'Flop' group, Nordström et al. 2025 octic-equivariant ViTs, Frank et al. 2024 RoPE-based Euclidean attention). The contribution is a recombination/extension of these lines rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming ('OMol25' vs 'OMolI25'), typos ('ProtienMD', 'Fabritiis' vs 'Fabritius'), and a few garbled reference entries ('Bekkers et al. 2024' abstract text is corrupted) reduce polish.

strengths: Elegant, principled design: defining RoPE attention relative to Platonic-solid reference frames and treating the |G| frames as parallel attention heads keeps the standard Transformer computation graph while injecting a geometric inductive bias, which is a clean and practical idea.

Strong theoretical grounding: the end-to-end equivariance proof (Prop. 3.1), the group-convolution characterization of equivariant linear layers (Eqs. 7-8), the dynamic-convolution equivalence of linear RoPE attention (Prop. 4.1), and the linear-time corollary are developed carefully and connected to established group theory (Appendices A-C).

Broad and diverse empirical validation spanning 2D vision (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), molecular property/force prediction and generation (QM9, OMol25), and proteins (ProteinMD), with results that are competitive or better against the controlled {e} baseline and several task-specific baselines.

The efficiency claims are backed by concrete evidence: matched-parameter design (holding C·|G| constant), wall-clock training-step timings (Table 11b) showing comparable forward/backward cost with reduced parameter-update overhead, and the Fourier-domain implementation (Appendix O) that shows real throughput gains at larger hidden dimensions.

Reproducibility is strong: open-source code, complete hyperparameter tables (Table 12), detailed per-dataset training recipes, and a candid limitations paragraph acknowledging uncharacterized extreme-scale behavior and restriction to O(n) subgroups.
weaknesses: Several headline comparisons are not compute-matched. On OMol25 the Platonic models (60M params) are compared against eSEN-sm (6M params); a 10x larger model being 2.6x faster and more accurate conflates architecture efficiency with model size, and FLOP counts are not reported, so the 'scalable and efficient' claim is not fully controlled.

The linear-time convolutional variant — a key selling point — is substantially worse than full attention (5.31 pp on CIFAR-10, 6.26 pp on ScanObjectNN), which undercuts its practical value; the linear-time result is therefore more a theoretical curiosity than a usable alternative at the reported scales.

Novelty is incremental: the equivariant linear layer is essentially standard group convolution / steerable-CNN weight sharing (Cohen & Welling 2016; Cohen et al. 2019), and the 'attention as dynamic convolution' connection parallels known linear-attention results. The contribution is mainly a synthesis of RoPE, group convolution, and Platonic frames rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

On non-equivariant vision tasks the model is far from SOTA (CIFAR-10 ~92%, ScanObjectNN ~86%), and only the trivial {e} baseline is used for comparison there; the paper does not establish competitiveness against modern point-cloud/image SOTA, so the 'competitive performance' framing rests on a narrow comparison.

The equivariant-vs-invariant attention ablation yields only a modest gain (0.01 vs 0.02 MAE on QM9-μ), and the dynamic-convolution equivalence requires restrictive assumptions (constant keys k_j=1, softmax omitted), limiting the strength of the 'learns adaptive geometric filters' narrative.

It is not fully disentangled whether gains on non-equivariant tasks come from genuine geometric equivariance or simply from symmetry-induced weight-sharing acting as a regularizer; the paper's own interpretation leans toward the latter, which weakens the geometric-bias motivation.

Only discrete subgroups of O(n) are supported, giving approximate E(n) equivariance; for molecular systems where full E(3)/SE(3) equivariance is the physical ideal, the approximation error (Appendix N.1) is not negligible, and its downstream impact is not quantified.
